summary: Cast-iron light first lit in 1883 at the tip of the Port de Grave Peninsula, Conception Bay; now owned by a heritage society.

lens.note: sixth-order lens in 1883 (LHF); present light not described beyond solar-charged batteries

structures.note: Coast Guard list 7.5 m; Peninsula page 6.3 m (20.7 ft)
torn down a few years after 1931 (LHF); taken apart and moved to Hussey's Cove (Heritage Society)

staffing.note: Solar-charged batteries; a nearby resident hired as caretaker after the dwelling was removed (LHF)

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (LHF). Road rough near the point; park near the last houses and walk about 1 km.

facts.owner: Port de Grave Peninsula Heritage Society (light and land transferred 5 August 2019)

events.note: Cast-iron tower erected early in 1883 on the community's request
Light placed in operation in 1883; a keeper appointed
Converted from kerosene to electricity; keeper no longer needed; dwelling removed a few years later
Recognized by Parks Canada as a heritage site, plaque installed (Peninsula page); LHF gives its heritage lighthouse status under the 2008 Act without a date
Light and surrounding land transferred to the Port de Grave Peninsula Heritage Society; Coast Guard keeps an operating presence

keepers.name: Robert Andrews
keepers.note: LHF calls him the first keeper (the light was lit in 1883) and its dated list reads 'at least 1886 - 1901'.

keepers.name: A. Andrews
keepers.note: Initial only in LHF's list; relation to Robert Andrews not stated

keepers.name: Richard Lear
keepers.note: LHF gives 'at least 1912'. The Heritage Society says he lived in the keeper's house beside the tower.

evidence.supports: Point is the eastern end of the Port de Grave Peninsula; commonly called Green Point
evidence.quote: Now commonly known as Green Point, Bay Roberts Point is the eastern end of the Port de Grave Peninsula

evidence.supports: Huntsman lost 28 April 1872 with 44 men in the Strait of Belle Isle
evidence.quote: On April 28, 1872, the Huntsman from Bay Roberts was lost in the Strait of Belle Isle along with its crew of forty-four men during the seal hunt.

evidence.supports: Peninsula page: 45 lives lost, Huntsman sank in a storm
evidence.quote: The story of this iconic lighthouse began with tragedy when the community of Bay Roberts suffered the devastating loss of 45 lives as the Huntsman vessel sank in a storm.

evidence.supports: Tower built at the community's request
evidence.quote: It was at the community’s behest that the classic cylindrical tower was constructed.

evidence.supports: 1880 petition to the House of Assembly
evidence.quote: In 1880, a petition from Isaac Bartlett and other residents of Bay Roberts and neighboring settlements on Conception Bay calling for the establishment of a lighthouse on Bay Roberts Point was presented to the Newfoundland House of Assembly.

evidence.supports: Inspector Neville 1882: four cast-iron towers prepared, one for Bay Roberts Point
evidence.quote: John T. Neville, Inspector of Lighthouses, noted in 1882 that four cast-iron towers had been prepared for harbour lights at Sandy Point, Point La Haye, Brigus, and Bay Roberts Point.

evidence.supports: 1882 store partly built under contract; tower in storage at Bay Roberts
evidence.quote: By the close of 1882, a store had been partially built on Green Point under contract, and the iron tower was in storage at Bay Roberts, ready to be sent to the point whenever the weather became sufficiently open for it to be erected.

evidence.supports: Early 1883 tower erected, keeper appointed, light placed in operation
evidence.quote: During the first part of 1883, the iron tower was put up on Green Point and equipped with its illuminating apparatus, a keeper was appointed, and the light was placed in operation.

evidence.supports: Red and white bands; fixed white light from a sixth-order lens
evidence.quote: The tower, which was painted with two red and three white horizontal bands, displayed a fixed white light using a sixth-order lens

evidence.supports: Three lamps in a projecting lantern: two white, centre red toward the southern rocks
evidence.quote: The two outer ones will show white , and the centre one, in a line with the Southern rocks

evidence.supports: Height 20.7 ft (6.3 m) per the peninsula page
evidence.quote: Since 1883 this red and white beacon has stood 20.7 feet (6.3 metres) tall

evidence.supports: Coast Guard list: LFl W 6s, focal height 17.1 m, range 7 nm, tower 7.5 m
evidence.quote: LFl W 6s 17.1 7 Cylindrical tower, red and white horizontal bands. 7.5

evidence.supports: Galvanized iron kerosene tank buried 1885
evidence.quote: A galvanized iron tank was partially buried at the station in 1885 to store the kerosene oil that was burned in the light.

evidence.supports: 1895 inspection report called for a porch on the keeper's house
evidence.quote: The inspection report for 1895 noted that a porch was required for the keeper�s house

evidence.supports: Robert Andrews of Ship Cove the first keeper
evidence.quote: The first keeper of the lighthouse was Robert Andrews of Ship Cove.

evidence.supports: Dated keeper list
evidence.quote: Keepers: Robert Andrews (at least 1886 - 1901), A. Andrews (1902 - 1903), Richard Lear (1904 - at least 1912), James Petten, Graham Petten, Richard French.

evidence.supports: Richard Lear lived in the keeper's house beside the light
evidence.quote: This is the house of the light house keeper next to the light house Richard Lear

evidence.supports: Keeper's house taken apart and moved to Hussey's Cove
evidence.quote: The house was later taken apart and brought to the Hussey’s Cove

evidence.supports: House still stands (society's account)
evidence.quote: The house still stands

evidence.supports: Converted to electricity 1931; dwelling torn down a few years later
evidence.quote: In 1931, the light was converted from kerosene to electricity, and a few years later the dwelling was torn down, as a resident keeper was no longer required for the automated light.

evidence.supports: Nearby resident hired as caretaker
evidence.quote: Instead, a nearby resident was hired to serve as a caretaker.

evidence.supports: Gallery: dwelling demolished after 1931 conversion
evidence.quote: The tower was originally adjoined to a keepers dwelling, however after the light was converted to electricity from kerosene in 1931 it was demolished as a full time keeper was no longer needed.

evidence.supports: Federal heritage 1990; heritage lighthouse under the 2008 Act (LHF text)
evidence.quote: The tower was classified a Recognized Federal Heritage Building in 1990, and then a Heritage Lighthouser under the Heritage Lighthouse Protection Act that was passed in 2008.

evidence.supports: Parks Canada recognition 2017 with plaque
evidence.quote: in 2017, Parks Canada recognized the Green Point Lighthouse as a Heritage Site, providing a plaque to mark the designation.

evidence.supports: Transfer to the Heritage Society celebrated 5 August 2019
evidence.quote: On August 5, 2019, the local community gathered to celebrate the transfer of Green Point Lighthouse and the surrounding land to the Port de Grave Peninsula Heritage Society.

evidence.supports: Society owns it; Coast Guard operating presence continues
evidence.quote: Now the property of the Port de Grave Heritage Society, the Coast Guard continues an operating presence

evidence.supports: Solar-charged batteries today
evidence.quote: Today, the light runs off solar-charged batteries.

evidence.supports: Automated and solar-powered (peninsula page)
evidence.quote: though today its light is automated and powered by solar energy

evidence.supports: Reserve engineers built viewing platforms and trails to the light
evidence.quote: constructing viewing platforms and developing walking trails leading down to the Green Point Lighthouse

evidence.supports: Grounds open, tower closed
evidence.quote: The lighthouse is owned by the Canadian Coast Guard. Grounds open, tower closed.

evidence.supports: Road directions and parking near the last houses, walk the last kilometre
evidence.quote: take a left onto a road opposite the harbour that will lead northeast toward Green Point Lighthouse

evidence.supports: Rough road; park near the last pair of houses and walk the last kilometre
evidence.quote: You will likely need to park near the last pair of houses and walk that last kilometer to the lighthouse as the road becomes quite rough and gradually disappears.

evidence.supports: Erected 1883 to serve the Port de Grave and Bay Roberts fishing communities
evidence.quote: Erected in 1883 to serve the fishing communities around Port De Grave and Bay Roberts

evidence.quote: at the rugged tip of the Port de Grave Peninsula

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Coast Guard list gives LFl W 6s (used in the record). Wikidata gives L Fl W 10s. LHF describes a fixed white light for the 1883 lamp, which is historical. Not reconciled; the list is the current authority.

LHF gives a Recognized Federal Heritage Building designation in 1990 and a heritage lighthouse status under the Heritage Lighthouse Protection Act (passed 2008); the Peninsula page gives 2017 as the Parks Canada heritage-site recognition. The record lists both 1990 and 2017; the dates describe different designations and the 2008 Act's date is not a designation date.
Peninsula page 6.3 m (20.7 ft); Coast Guard list 7.5 m; the record's 9.0 m from the Parks Canada listing was not confirmed by any source read. Not reconciled.

notes_for_editor: Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Huntsman paragraph no longer says the light was built after the loss, because the only link is the Peninsula page's 'began with tragedy' wording and LHF places the wreck in the Strait of Belle Isle, not at the point; the record's summary had repeated the causal link and is corrected. 'Rocky tip' (no source) is now 'rugged tip' (Peninsula page). 'Lit since 1883' is now 'first lit in 1883'. The 1990 and 2017 designations are stated as possibly different designations. Story shape is moderate: four chapters (The place, Building the light, The keepers, Today). The 1931 end of resident keeping sits in The keepers and the designations and 2019 transfer sit in Today, because the story's shape rule allows at most four chapters for a moderate station; After the keepers has no separate heading. Moderate-to-thin station. The Parks Canada Directory of Federal Heritage Designations statement of significance (page 15417) is script-rendered and gave no text through fetch_text, so it is not cited. Search snippets quoting it give 6.3 m, 1883, and a Huntsman loss of 45 men at the community's request; the same 45-man figure is in the Peninsula page, which is cited. If the Parks Canada text is wanted, check it by hand. The Huntsman: LHF says 44 men in the Strait of Belle Isle during the seal hunt; the Peninsula page says 45 lives in a storm. No contemporary account was found in the corpus or in Chronicling America (the 1872 search returned only OCR junk), so the loss is stated as two accounts. The 1883 keeper appointment is in LHF's text, but the first keeper's start year is not dated, so Robert Andrews' from-year is the 1883 appointment as LHF's first-keeper claim. The Peninsula page says 'nearby residents have staffed the lighthouse for generations', which conflicts with LHF (resident keeper not needed after 1931). Not used. The Heritage Society's account names private residents of the moved house; those names are left out. The 2019 transfer and the Coast Guard presence are both stated, with the Society's page as the later source. Historic Newfoundland light lists were not in the corpus, so the 1883 lamp description is LHF's citation of the Light List.
